reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: A malignant cartilage-forming bone tumour, usually of middle-aged and older adults, most often affecting the pelvis, proximal femur, humerus, and axial skeleton

Conventional chondrosarcoma may arise de novo or secondarily within a pre-existing enchondroma or osteochondroma, and multiplicity raises the possibility of enchondromatosis or hereditary multiple exostoses
Radiographs typically show a lytic lesion with characteristic ring-and-arc or popcorn cartilage matrix mineralisation, endosteal scalloping, and cortical involvement
Distinguishing a low-grade chondrosarcoma from a benign enchondroma is a classic diagnostic challenge that relies on combined clinical, radiological, and pathological assessment
Conventional chondrosarcomas frequently harbour IDH1 or IDH2 mutations, a helpful molecular clue, while mesenchymal chondrosarcoma carries a HEY1-NCOA2 fusion
Because the tumour is largely resistant to conventional radiotherapy and chemotherapy, complete surgical excision with adequate margins is the mainstay of treatment
Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma, in which a high-grade non-cartilaginous component develops, behaves very aggressively with a poor prognosis
Staging includes local MRI, plain radiographs, and chest CT for pulmonary metastases
reference.pathophysiology: Chondrosarcoma is a malignant tumour whose cells produce a cartilaginous matrix. Conventional tumours are frequently associated with mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase genes IDH1 or IDH2, which generate an oncometabolite that alters cellular epigenetics and disturbs chondrocyte differentiation. Tumours may arise de novo or through malignant change in benign cartilage lesions such as enchondromas or osteochondromas. The relatively avascular, matrix-rich nature of cartilaginous tumours limits the delivery and efficacy of chemotherapy and radiotherapy, explaining their characteristic treatment resistance. Higher-grade and dedifferentiated tumours acquire further genetic alterations that confer aggressive behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Enchondroma and other benign cartilage tumours
Osteochondroma with a thickened cartilage cap
Fibrous dysplasia or bone infarct with matrix mineralisation
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs to assess matrix mineralisation, endosteal scalloping, and cortical destruction
MRI of the affected bone to define soft-tissue extent and marrow involvement
CT to characterise matrix mineralisation and cortical integrity
Image-guided biopsy with careful tract planning, recognising the difficulty of grading cartilage tumours on limited samples
Molecular testing for IDH1/IDH2 mutations or, in mesenchymal chondrosarcoma, HEY1-NCOA2 fusion where indicated
redFlags: New or progressive deep pain in a known cartilage lesion, especially at night or at rest
Enlargement of a previously stable enchondroma or osteochondroma, or a thick cartilage cap on an exostosis
A destructive axial or pelvic lytic lesion with a soft-tissue mass
Rapid clinical deterioration suggesting a dedifferentiated high-grade component
Pathological fracture through a cartilaginous lesion
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is governed principally by histological grade and completeness of resection; low-grade tumours have an excellent outcome after adequate surgery, whereas high-grade, dedifferentiated, and axial or pelvic tumours that are difficult to resect completely carry a markedly worse prognosis.
pitfalls: Overlooking a low-grade chondrosarcoma by mistaking it for a benign enchondroma, or vice versa
Expecting response to radiotherapy or chemotherapy in conventional disease, which is largely resistant
Undersampling a heterogeneous tumour and missing a dedifferentiated high-grade area
Inadequate surgical margins leading to local recurrence
Poor biopsy tract planning that jeopardises subsequent limb-sparing or complex axial resection
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Complete surgical excision with adequate margins is the mainstay, as conventional chondrosarcoma is largely resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy
Manage low-grade appendicular tumours with wide resection or extended intralesional curettage, reserving wide en bloc resection for higher-grade lesions
Use radiotherapy, including proton or particle therapy, for unresectable or incompletely resected axial and skull base tumours
Add systemic chemotherapy for the more chemosensitive mesenchymal and dedifferentiated subtypes
Consider IDH-directed targeted therapy within trials for IDH1 or IDH2-mutant tumours
Undertake long-term surveillance for local recurrence and pulmonary metastases with cross-sectional and chest imaging
Manage through a specialist bone sarcoma multidisciplinary team
